simpexp

Simulate single-event, competing-risks and multi-state event histories from hazards that are piecewise constant on a time grid.

Each transition is specified by a formula for its log-hazard. Because the hazards are piecewise constant by construction, waiting times are drawn by inverting the cumulative hazard in closed form, and the realised transition is drawn with probabilities proportional to the transition-specific hazards inside the interval in which the event falls. No quadrature, no interpolated inverse, no rejection sampling — the grid is part of the model, not a tuning parameter.

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("adibender/simpexp")

Three interfaces, one engine 

library(simpexp)
df  <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500))
cut <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)

# single event, hazard rising over time
sim_pexp(~ log(0.1) + 0.05 * t + 0.3 * x, df, cut)

# competing risks: one formula per cause
sim_pexp_cr(list(relapse = ~ log(0.1) + 0.3 * x, death = ~ log(0.05)), df, cut)

# multi state, here illness-death with recovery
sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",     ~ log(0.4) + 0.3 * x),
    transition("healthy", "dead",    ~ log(0.02)),
    transition("ill",     "healthy", ~ log(0.8) - 0.25 * t_sojourn),
    transition("ill",     "dead",    ~ log(0.05) + 0.15 * t_sojourn)
  ),
  df, cut)

All three return the same long format, one row per episode:

id episode from to tstart tstop status transition …

status = 0 marks an episode that ended without a transition, with to missing.

Markov, semi-Markov, neither

What a hazard may depend on is what distinguishes the three cases, and it is simply a matter of which variable the formula uses:

variable meaning process
t (= tend) time since the origin Markov
t_sojourn time in the current state semi-Markov
t_entry time the current state was entered neither
n_visits_<state> visits to a state so far neither
t_total_<state> time spent in a state so far neither
n_transitions transitions so far neither
interval index of the current interval of cut — 
# the hazard of dying rises with every previous illness episode
transition("ill", "dead", ~ log(0.02) + 0.5 * n_visits_ill)

keep_history = TRUE returns these features with the episodes. They are the ground truth of the process, which makes them the oracle features of a simulation study.

Censoring

Follow-up ends at the last value of cut, which censors administratively. Anything earlier is added afterwards:

sim <- sim_pexp(~ log(0.2) + 0.3 * x, df, cut)
add_censoring(sim, rate = 0.1)              # exponential censoring times
add_censoring(sim, times = runif(500, 2, 10))  # given times, e.g. staggered entry

Censoring that depends on covariates or on the state of the process is better expressed as part of the process itself — a transition into a censoring state, competing with the others:

sim_pexp_msm(
  list(transition("0", "event", ~ log(0.3)),
       transition("0", "lost",  ~ log(0.1) + 0.5 * x)),
  df, cut, censoring_states = "lost")

Validation

Every claim above is checked against something independent. The article Validation against other simulators implements the same data-generating process in simpexp and in another package, fits one and the same model to both samples, and compares the estimates with each other and with the closed form where one exists:

case reference
single event, piecewise constant hazard msm::rpexp
single event, Weibull hazard simsurv (inversion of the continuous hazard)
competing risks closed-form probabilities, latent failure times
multi-state, Markov msm::sim.msm, with an msm model fitted to both
multi-state, semi-Markov gems

Fitting back what was simulated

The hazards are specified under the same convention under which piecewise exponential additive models are fitted — constant on (tstart, tend], evaluated at tend — so a model fitted to the simulated data estimates the quantity that was specified. tests/testthat/test-roundtrip.R does exactly that: expand the episodes into intervals, fit a Poisson model with log exposure as offset, and recover the coefficients.

Relation to pammtools

The simulation functions of pammtools are the origin of this package. This package is developed independently of them: it shares no code and no dependency in either direction, so simulation and model fitting are no longer tied to each other. pammtools keeps its own sim_pexp() for now.
